games.explanation: Nola's platoon split is the whole story here, and the market is pricing this like it doesn't exist. He turns into a batting-practice arm against lefties, and Toronto happens to run out a lineup full of them behind Springer, who has been the best bat in this game all year. Wind blowing out at 15 in a park that already juices homers by 21 percent is not the environment you want when your right-hander is giving up barrels to lefties at a 13 percent clip. Scherzer isn't the Scherzer of old, but he doesn't need to be in a slugfest the board refuses to acknowledge. Getting +149 on the better team in the better spot is the kind of price that doesn't survive first pitch.

Bubba Chandler's overall line looks tidy right up until you split it by handedness, at which point the rookie's problem with right-handed bats jumps off the page. The Mets happen to run a righty-heavy top of the order that punishes exactly that weakness, with Lindor and Bichette both carrying xwOBAs north of .345 against right-handed pitching. Pittsburgh's counter is a lineup where the two dangerous bats strike out nearly 27% of the time, which is not the recipe for surviving nine innings as the better team's underdog. The board has this as a coin flip and is charging you plus money to take the side with the deeper roster and the better matchup. +125 on the stronger club is the whole argument.

Cleveland is the home team and the shorter price, but Gavin Williams walks the ballpark and gives up loud contact when hitters do connect, which is not the profile you want against a lineup built around left-handed thump and free passes. The White Sox draw a starter whose double-digit walk rate plays right into Vargas and Montgomery, the latter posting a .358 xwOBA against righties this year. Cleveland's counter is a top three that leans heavily on Ramirez and a Kwan who slaps singles and little else, hardly the group to bury you in a projected one-run game. Getting plus money on the better team in a coin-flip script is the entire angle, and +120 is generous for what our model sees as a near six-point mispricing.

Yamamoto is the kind of name that anchors a price whether or not the matchup deserves it, and tonight the market is charging full freight against a Diamondbacks lineup that actually gives him trouble. Arizona runs four right-handed bats at the top who all sit north of a .345 xwOBA, and Yamamoto's numbers against righties are noticeably softer than his overall line suggests. Pfaadt is the obvious hole in the argument, but the sim still lands on a one-run game because the Dodgers beyond Ohtani are more ordinary than the logo implies. Getting +162 on a coin flip the market has priced as a mismatch is the entire trade.

Kirby's reputation still gets him priced like an ace, but the underlying contact he allows has been closer to a mid-rotation arm all year, and Tampa happens to have the exact right-handed bats to exploit it. Aranda has been demolishing righties with a .410 xwOBA, and Díaz and Caminero round out a top of the order built to punish hard-hit contact allowers. Jax on the other side brings a strikeout rate north of 35%, which is the fastest way to neutralize a Seattle lineup that swings and misses plenty. Getting plus money on the better team, with the better bats for the matchup, is the whole story here.
